competent.path: Competent comes from Latin competere, to strive together or be fit for something, joining com- with petere, to seek. It describes someone adequately skilled, suited to the task they're seeking to do.

complacent.path: Complacent comes from Latin complacere, to please greatly, joining the intensive com- with placere, to please. Someone complacent is so thoroughly pleased with themselves that they become smugly unaware of danger.

complaisance.path: Complaisance shares complacent's root, Latin complacere, to please greatly. Where complacent turned inward to self-satisfaction, complaisance kept the outward sense: an eagerness to please others.

complaisant.path: Complaisant shares the same Latin root, complacere, to please greatly. It describes someone willing and eager to please, obliging toward others' wishes.

complement.path: Complement comes from Latin complere, to fill up completely, joining com- with plere, to fill. To complement something is to fill it out, completing or enhancing it.

complementary.path: Complementary shares complement's root, Latin complere, to fill up. Complementary things combine to fill each other out, forming a complete whole together.

compliant.path: Compliant comes from the same Latin root as complement, complere, to fill up or fulfill. Someone compliant fulfills what's asked of them, readily obeying or conforming to a rule or request.

complicit.path: Complicit comes from Latin complicare, to fold together, the same root as accomplice and complicated. To be complicit is to be folded into, entangled with, others in wrongdoing.

comply.path: Comply traces through Italian complire back to Latin complere, to fill up or fulfill. To comply is to fulfill a rule or request, acting in accordance with it.

comport.path: Comport comes from Latin comportare, to carry together, joining com- with portare, to carry. To comport oneself is to carry oneself in a certain way; to comport with something is for it to align with it.

compound.path: Compound comes from Latin componere, to put together, joining com- with ponere, to place. To compound a problem is to put more onto it, piling addition upon addition until it worsens.

comprehensive.path: Comprehensive comes from Latin comprehendere, to grasp together, joining com- with prehendere, to seize. Something comprehensive grasps every part at once: complete, covering everything.

compromise.path: Compromise comes from Latin compromittere, joining com-, together, with promittere, to promise, originally a mutual pledge to accept an arbiter's decision. It settled into meaning a mutual settlement by concession, or, more darkly, to endanger something by weakening it.

concede.path: Concede comes from Latin concedere, joining con- with cedere, to yield or go. To concede is to yield ground: to admit or surrender something, often reluctantly.

conceit.literal: a thing conceived, taken up in the mind
conceit.path: Conceit comes from Latin concipere, to conceive, joining con- with capere, to take or seize: literally an idea taken up in the mind. It split into two senses: an elaborate literary idea or metaphor, and an overblown idea of one's own worth, excessive pride.

concept.literal: a thing taken up in the mind
concept.path: Concept shares conceit's root, Latin concipere, to conceive, from con- and capere, to take. It names an abstract idea formed and held in the mind: a general notion.

concern.path: Concern comes from Latin concernere, to sift together or relate to, joining con- with cernere, to distinguish or perceive. What concerns you is sifted out as relevant to you, whether as worry or simple interest.

conciliate.path: Conciliate comes from Latin conciliare, to bring together, from concilium, a council or assembly summoned together. To conciliate is to call opposing sides back together: to win over or reconcile.

conciliatory.path: Conciliatory shares conciliate's root, Latin concilium, an assembly called together. It describes an approach intended to placate and bring opposing sides back into agreement.

conclusive.path: Conclusive comes from Latin concludere, to close up or conclude, joining con- with claudere, to shut. A conclusive argument shuts the door on the matter entirely, ending all doubt.

concomitant.path: Concomitant comes from Latin comes, a companion, joined with con-, together. It describes something that travels alongside another as its companion: occurring together with it.

concur.path: Concur comes from Latin concurrere, to run together, joining con- with currere, to run. Minds that concur run together toward the same point: they agree.

condemn.path: Condemn comes from Latin condemnare, joining the intensive con- with damnare, to harm or condemn, from damnum, harm. To condemn is to pronounce strong disapproval, or formally to sentence someone to harm.

condolence.path: Condolence comes from Latin condolere, to suffer together, joining con- with dolere, to grieve. It names an expression of sympathy that shares, in words, another person's grief.

condone.path: Condone comes from Latin condonare, to forgive or remit entirely, joining con- with donare, to give, from donum, a gift. To condone wrongdoing is to freely give it a pass: overlooking or tacitly accepting it.

conducive.path: Conducive comes from Latin conducere, to lead together, joining con- with ducere, to lead. Something conducive leads you toward a favorable result, tending to promote or help bring it about.

conduct.path: Conduct shares conducive's root, Latin conducere, to lead. As a noun it names the way a person leads or carries themselves: their behavior.

confer.path: Confer comes from Latin conferre, to bring together, joining con- with ferre, to carry. To confer is either to bring ideas together in discussion, or to bring and bestow something, like an honor, upon someone.

conflagration.path: Conflagration comes from Latin conflagrare, to burn up completely, joining the intensive con- with flagrare, to blaze. It names a large, destructive fire that burns everything in its path.

conflate.path: Conflate comes from Latin conflare, to blow together and fuse, as a smith blows air on a fire to melt metals into one. To conflate two things is to blow them together into a single, confused whole.

confluence.path: Confluence comes from Latin confluere, to flow together, joining con- with fluere, to flow, as two rivers merge into one. It names any coming together, literal or figurative, of separate streams into one.

confound.path: Confound comes from Latin confundere, to pour things together and mix them up, joining con- with fundere, to pour. To confound someone is to pour their thoughts into confusion: to baffle or thwart them.

congeal.path: Congeal comes from Latin congelare, to freeze together, joining con- with gelare, to freeze, from gelu, frost. It describes anything that solidifies, especially by cooling, as if freezing into one mass.

parts.meaning: of the same birth or nature

congenial.literal: of the same birth or nature
congenial.path: Congenial joins con-, together, with genialis, of the same birth or nature, from genius, one's inborn character. People who are congenial share a compatible nature: pleasant and agreeable in company.

conjectural.path: Conjectural comes from Latin conicere, to throw together and so infer or guess, joining con- with iacere, to throw. A conjectural claim is one thrown together from guesswork rather than solid evidence.

conjugal.path: Conjugal comes from Latin conjunx, a spouse, from conjungere, to join together, joining con- with iungere, to yoke or join. It describes anything relating to the union of marriage.

conjure.path: Conjure comes from Latin conjurare, to swear a solemn oath together, joining con- with iurare, to swear. That binding oath became the ritual invocation of a magician, and to conjure is to summon something as if by a magic spell.

conniving.path: Connive comes from Latin connivere, to shut the eyes or wink, joining con- with a root meaning to close the eyes. To connive was originally to look the other way at wrongdoing, and shifted to actively scheming: conniving.

connoisseur.path: Connoisseur comes from French connaitre, to know, from Latin cognoscere, to know thoroughly. It names an expert judge, someone who truly knows a subject, especially matters of taste.

connotation.path: Connotation joins con-, together, with notare, to mark, from nota, a sign. A connotation is a meaning marked onto a word alongside its literal sense: an implied meaning beyond the literal.

connote.path: Connote shares connotation's root, con-, together, and notare, to mark. To connote is to carry an implied meaning alongside the literal one.

conscientious.path: Conscientious comes from Latin conscientia, inner knowledge or conscience, joining con- with scire, to know. Someone conscientious acts from that inner knowing of right and wrong: careful, thorough, and guided by principle.

consecrate.path: Consecrate comes from Latin consecrare, joining the intensive con- with sacrare, to make sacred, from sacer, sacred. To consecrate is to declare something sacred, dedicating it solemnly to a higher purpose.

consensus.path: Consensus comes from Latin consentire, to feel together, joining con- with sentire, to feel or perceive, the root of sense and sentiment. A consensus is a shared feeling: general agreement within a group.

consequential.path: Consequential comes from Latin consequi, to follow closely with something, joining con- with sequi, to follow. A consequential event is one whose effects follow significantly, mattering in what comes after.

conservatory.path: Conservatory comes from Latin conservare, to preserve carefully, joining con- with servare, to keep. A conservatory was first a place for preserving delicate plants, extended to a place preserving and cultivating musical talent.

consider.path: Consider probably comes from Latin considerare, to observe the stars closely, joining con- with sidus, a star, an old term from augury or astrology. Careful stargazing became careful thought in general: to think about something carefully.

console.path: Console comes from Latin consolari, to comfort greatly, joining the intensive con- with solari, to soothe. To console someone is to comfort them in their distress.

consolidate.path: Consolidate comes from Latin consolidare, to make firm, joining con- with solidus, solid. To consolidate is to combine separate parts into one solid, stronger whole.

conspicuous.path: Conspicuous comes from Latin conspicere, to look at closely, joining the intensive con- with specere, to look. Something conspicuous is so easy to look at, so clearly visible, that it attracts notice.
